  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Good morning, listeners tuning in across the United States, and welcome to Audexa Radio. I'm Alex, and today we're taking a deeper look at AI beyond the shiny demos: workplace culture, security, and the very real question of whether these systems are ready to be trusted.","type":"intro"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"And I'm Jordan. The interesting thread running through several of today's discussions is that AI progress isn't just about bigger models. It's also about the people building them, the software surrounding them, and the assumptions we make when an AI system appears confident.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Let's start with a headline that got a lot of attention on Hacker News: a former OpenAI employee saying, bluntly, that the company's culture is broken. Now, that is a strong claim. What should listeners take from it without turning one person's account into the entire story?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"The useful takeaway is less about judging one company and more about understanding the pressure inside frontier AI labs. These organizations are trying to move quickly while also handling safety research, enormous financial expectations, and products that can affect millions of people. When employees describe internal disagreement, shifting priorities, or concerns about whether safety work is genuinely valued, that tells us governance is part of the technology story.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So when someone says the culture is broken, the question for the public is: broken in what way? Is it about long hours, leadership, safety decisions, or the tension between research and launching products?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Exactly. And listeners should look for specifics: Were safety reviews bypassed? Could researchers raise concerns without retaliation? Were product deadlines given priority over testing? Those questions are more informative than a dramatic label. The broader implication is that AI reliability depends partly on institutional reliability. A model can be technically impressive, but if the organization around it discourages criticism, problems may remain hidden until they reach users.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"That brings us neatly to another major story: Linux kernel developer Greg Kroah-Hartman's discussion of security in the LLM age. This feels especially relevant because so many developers now use AI to write, explain, or modify code.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Right. The central security lesson is simple: generated code is still code written by an untrusted assistant. It can be useful, fast, and often correct, but it doesn't understand your entire threat model. An AI may suggest a library with a known vulnerability, mishandle authentication, expose sensitive information in logs, or produce code that passes a basic test while failing under adversarial input.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And that applies outside professional software teams, too. If a listener asks an AI to automate a spreadsheet, build a personal website, or connect two services, they may be creating something that handles passwords or private data without realizing the risks.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Precisely. The practical rule is to treat AI output like a fast first draft from a junior contributor. Review it, test it, check dependencies, and keep secrets out of prompts. For companies, that means code scanning, access controls, human approval for sensitive changes, and clear policies about what data can be sent to an AI service. The technology can raise productivity, but it also lowers the barrier to producing insecure software at scale.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Now let's tackle the more philosophical debate. Yann LeCun has said he has zero concerns about AI wiping out humanity, even as researchers and users continue reporting so-called rogue or unexpected model behavior. Is this mostly a disagreement about terminology?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Partly. LeCun is skeptical of the idea that current systems are on a direct path to autonomous human extinction. Other researchers focus on nearer-term risks: fraud, cyberattacks, dangerous instructions, manipulation, and systems taking actions they weren't intended to take. Both sides can be discussing real issues while using different definitions of danger.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So the phrase rogue AI can make people picture a movie villain, when the actual problem might be a model confidently doing the wrong thing inside a business workflow.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Exactly. A model doesn't need consciousness or a secret plan to cause damage. It only needs access, a vague objective, and insufficient oversight. An agent that books appointments, edits files, sends email, or operates software can create trouble through ordinary mistakes. That suggests a less dramatic but more useful safety approach: limit permissions, require confirmation for high-impact actions, log decisions, and design systems so one bad output doesn't cascade into a major failure.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And that may be the common thread across all three stories. Don't just ask whether the model is smart. Ask who built the system, what it can access, and what happens when it gets something wrong.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"That's the key. AI is becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure needs accountability. For listeners using these tools today, the best habits are surprisingly practical: verify important claims, review generated code, protect confidential information, and keep a human in the loop whenever money, safety, privacy, or reputation is involved.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Great conversation. AI isn't slowing down, but the smarter way to use it may be to slow down just enough to check the work. You're listening to Audexa Radio, and we'll be right back after this track.","type":"outro"}
]

  {"speaker":"host1","text":"All right, listeners tuning in to Audexa Radio, we just got a call from a listener who wants to hear about how black holes form. That is a fantastic request, because we're about to talk about some of the most extreme objects in the universe.","type":"listener_request"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Absolutely. And let's start with the basic idea: a black hole forms when a huge amount of matter gets squeezed into an incredibly small region of space. The gravity becomes so strong that, past a boundary called the event horizon, not even light can escape.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So we're not talking about a cosmic vacuum cleaner cruising around and sucking up everything nearby?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Exactly. That's one of the biggest myths. From a safe distance, a black hole's gravity behaves much like the gravity of any other object with the same mass. The danger comes when matter gets extremely close, where the gravitational pull becomes overwhelming.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Now, the most familiar route to forming a black hole begins with a massive star, right?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Right. A very massive star spends its life balancing two forces. Fusion in its core produces outward pressure, while gravity pulls everything inward. For millions of years, those forces can hold each other in check. But eventually, the star runs out of fuel it can fuse efficiently, and that support starts to collapse.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And then the star's core essentially caves in?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"In a spectacular and violent way. The core collapses in a fraction of a second, while the outer layers can blast into space in a supernova explosion. If the remaining core is massive enough, gravity continues crushing it down until a black hole forms.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"What determines whether the leftover core becomes a black hole or something else, like a neutron star?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Mass is the key factor, though the details involve the star's composition, rotation, and how much material it loses before the explosion. A lighter remnant may settle as a neutron star, where matter is incredibly dense but still has a surface. A heavier remnant can collapse beyond that point and create an event horizon.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"But stellar collapse isn't the only way black holes can grow, is it?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"No. Once a black hole exists, it can gain mass by pulling in gas, dust, planets, or stars. If material spirals toward it, friction can heat that material to enormous temperatures, creating a glowing accretion disk. In some systems, that disk shines brighter than entire galaxies, even though the black hole itself emits no light.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And then there are the giants at the centers of galaxies: supermassive black holes.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Exactly. These can contain millions or even billions of times the Sun's mass. Scientists are still studying how the earliest supermassive black holes formed so quickly in the young universe. Possibilities include the collapse of enormous early stars, dense clouds of gas collapsing directly, and rapid growth through mergers and accretion.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So black holes can be born from dying stars, and then they can grow by feeding on their surroundings and merging with other black holes. Cosmic recycling, but with much higher stakes.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"That's a good way to put it. And when two black holes merge, they send ripples through space-time called gravitational waves. Observatories on Earth can detect those ripples, giving us a new way to study black holes without seeing them directly.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"What a question to send our way. Thanks to our listener for that request, and for giving us a reason to take a quick trip to the edge of space-time. You're listening to Audexa Radio, live.","type":"outro"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"And remember, black holes aren't empty holes in space; they're regions where matter has collapsed so intensely that gravity reshapes the rules of escape. Stick around, we've got more coming up after this track.","type":"transition"}
]

  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Good morning, listeners tuning in across the United States — you’re with Alex and Jordan on Audexa Radio. Today’s deep dive is all about science that sounds futuristic, but could affect the way we drive, think, and even search for life beyond Earth.","type":"intro"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"We’re focusing on three stories: privacy in connected cars, a possible clue to the universe’s expansion mystery, and the remarkable chemistry of ocean spray from Saturn’s moon Enceladus. Different subjects, but they share one theme: hidden systems revealing themselves through data.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Let’s start close to home — literally in the car sitting in your driveway. A data-privacy study called Automatic Transmission looks at connected vehicles and the information they collect. Jordan, what exactly are we talking about here?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Modern vehicles can gather far more than location. Depending on the model and its services, data may include driving behavior, vehicle diagnostics, phone connections, infotainment activity, and sometimes information associated with the people using the car. Much of that data supports useful features — navigation, emergency assistance, maintenance alerts — but the study raises a basic question: who controls the information once it leaves the vehicle?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And that’s the part that makes people sit up. We used to think of a car as a machine that got us from point A to point B. Now it’s more like a smartphone on wheels — except many drivers may not realize how much they’ve agreed to share.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Exactly. The practical implication is that privacy isn’t just about whether a company has your name. Patterns can be revealing. Regular routes might suggest where someone lives or works. Sudden changes in driving could expose travel habits. Data can also pass through manufacturers, app providers, insurers, or service partners. The study doesn’t mean every connected car is secretly spying on its owner, but it does show why clearer consent and stronger limits matter.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So what can listeners do right now? Are we supposed to go out and disconnect the entire dashboard?","type":"listener_request"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Not necessarily. Start with the vehicle’s privacy settings and the companion app. Check which services are active, whether location sharing is required, and what happens when you sell or return the car. Remove old phones and user profiles, too. And when buying a vehicle, ask a simple question: what data does it collect, who receives it, and how long is it retained?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"That’s a good consumer checklist — and honestly, it’s a reminder that convenience always comes with a data footprint. Now let’s zoom way out, past the highway and into the universe.","type":"transition"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Astronomers are still wrestling with a major disagreement over how quickly the universe is expanding. Different methods produce different answers, a problem often called the Hubble tension. New simulations suggest that tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may have influenced the distribution of matter and light in ways that affect our measurements.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"That sounds like the cosmic version of finding a hidden setting that changes the whole calculation. Are these primordial magnetic fields a confirmed answer?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"No — and that distinction is important. They’re a possible explanation, not a solved case. The idea is that early magnetic fields could have shaped cosmic structure or altered signals that astronomers use as a ruler. If so, some of the disagreement might come from overlooking that influence. Researchers will need observations from telescopes and other experiments to test whether the predicted patterns are really there.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So even a tiny field from the universe’s infancy could complicate a measurement billions of years later. That’s humbling — and a little rude of the cosmos.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Science is full of those surprises. And our final story takes us to Enceladus, an icy moon of Saturn. Beneath its frozen crust is a global ocean, and cracks near the south pole spray water vapor and ice particles into space. Researchers are finding that those particles can become chemically diverse ice grains, carrying clues from the ocean below.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Which means a spacecraft might be able to study an alien ocean without drilling through miles of ice. That’s incredible. What can those grains tell scientists?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"They can reveal the chemistry of the hidden ocean, including salts, organic molecules, and possibly the conditions around its seafloor. The particles don’t all form in the same way, so their variety may preserve information about temperature, pressure, and chemical reactions. It’s not evidence of life, but it tells us Enceladus has ingredients and environments worth investigating.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And that’s the bigger picture: a privacy study tells us to look carefully at the invisible systems in our cars; cosmology reminds us that tiny effects can reshape enormous conclusions; and Enceladus shows that an ocean can advertise its secrets by spraying them into space.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Right. The exciting part of science isn’t just discovering something new. It’s learning how to read signals that were always there — data from a vehicle, light from the early universe, or ice grains drifting above an alien moon.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"What a journey — from your driveway to Saturn before breakfast. Thanks for tuning in to this science deep dive on Audexa Radio. Stay curious, check those car privacy settings, and we’ll be right back after this track.","type":"outro"}
]

  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So for listeners who have always said, \"I'd love to make a game, but I don't know where to begin,\" this is the kind of thing that might actually get them started?","type":"listener_request"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Absolutely. You won't be building the next blockbuster open-world game with it, and that's the point. You can make a small arcade game, a puzzle game, or a short narrative experiment and understand the entire pipeline. That kind of ownership is powerful. It also reflects a broader indie trend: tools are becoming more welcoming, while developers are choosing focused projects over years-long production cycles.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Now, speaking of ambitious experiments, here's one that sounds like it escaped from a hacker convention: a space game with a built-in RISC-V emulator that runs Linux. Yes, inside the game. I have questions, Jordan. First one: why?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Because programmers are constitutionally incapable of leaving a perfectly good computer architecture alone. More seriously, the project is a great example of games becoming platforms for technical curiosity. A RISC-V emulator allows the game to simulate another processor, and running Linux inside that environment turns the fictional spacecraft into a programmable sandbox. It isn't necessarily a feature most players need, but it creates possibilities for modding, automation, education, and emergent gameplay.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"That sounds like the kind of game where the official objective is explore the galaxy, but the real objective is spend six hours trying to boot an operating system in your spaceship.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"And then proudly announce that it worked, even though nobody asked. But this is important because these projects challenge the idea that games have to be tightly scripted products. They can be laboratories, toolboxes, or social spaces. Newgrounds gives people a creative community, Pyxel gives them accessible production tools, and the RISC-V project gives players a programmable world to investigate.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So the common thread isn't just retro graphics or clever engineering. It's control. Smaller creators and curious players are getting more ways to shape the experience themselves, whether that's making a game, remixing art, or literally installing Linux in a virtual spaceship.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"That's the big takeaway. Alongside the huge releases and billion-dollar franchises, there's a healthy layer of experimentation that keeps gaming inventive. AAA games may dominate the headlines, but projects like these often influence how the next generation of developers learns, builds, and thinks about interactive entertainment.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"I love that. Big worlds, tiny teams, and at least one person determined to turn a spaceship into a very complicated laptop. Thanks for the tour, Jordan. Listeners tuning in to Audexa Radio, don't go anywhere—we'll be right back after this track.","type":"outro"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"And when we return, we'll keep exploring the games and ideas pushing the medium in unexpected directions. Stay with us.","type":"transition"}
]

[
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"We just got a call from a listener who wants to hear about why mortgage rates move when the Fed meets. Great question, and thanks for calling Audexa Radio! Listeners tuning in this morning, let’s break down what’s really happening behind those rate headlines.","type":"listener_request"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Absolutely. The first thing to know is that the Federal Reserve does not directly set the interest rate on a typical thirty-year mortgage. The Fed sets a short-term policy rate, which influences the cost of borrowing between banks. Mortgage rates are tied more closely to longer-term bond markets, especially the yield on ten-year U.S. Treasury bonds.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So when the Fed meets, it’s not like someone presses a button labeled mortgage rates and suddenly every home loan changes?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Exactly. The connection is indirect, but powerful. Investors listen carefully for what the Fed says about inflation, economic growth, and future interest-rate decisions. If they think the Fed will keep rates high for longer, bond yields may rise, and mortgage rates often move higher too. If they expect rate cuts ahead, yields can fall, which may pull mortgage rates down.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And sometimes mortgage rates move before the Fed even announces anything, right?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"They do. Markets are constantly reacting to economic reports, speeches from Fed officials, inflation data, and job numbers. By the time the Fed meeting arrives, investors may already have priced in much of the expected decision. That means the biggest mortgage-rate movement can happen when the Fed surprises markets, or when its forecast and language suggest a different path than investors expected.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Let’s put that into real-life terms. Say the Fed holds its policy rate steady. That doesn’t necessarily mean mortgage rates stay frozen, does it?","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Not at all. A steady Fed decision can still lead to higher or lower mortgage rates depending on the message around it. If the Fed says inflation remains stubborn and future cuts may be delayed, mortgage rates could rise. If officials signal confidence that inflation is cooling and rate cuts are becoming more likely, mortgage rates could ease—even though the current policy rate hasn’t changed.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And there’s another piece here: mortgage lenders are thinking about risk. They’re looking at investor demand, the economy, and whether borrowers are likely to keep making payments. So the final rate on a loan includes more than just the Fed story.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Right. Lenders also consider the borrower’s credit score, down payment, loan type, property, and market conditions. A person with excellent credit and a larger down payment may receive a very different offer from someone with a smaller down payment. That’s why consumers should compare multiple lenders and look at both the interest rate and the annual percentage rate, or APR, which includes certain fees.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"So the quick takeaway: the Fed influences mortgage rates, but it doesn’t control them directly. Markets react not just to today’s decision, but to what investors think happens next.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"That’s the key idea. Think of a Fed meeting as a major signal for the economy, not a direct mortgage-rate remote control. And if you’re shopping for a home, try not to make a decision based on one day’s headline. Budget for the payment you can comfortably afford, ask about locking your rate, and get professional advice for your situation.","type":"listener_request"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Great explanation, Jordan—and thanks again to our caller for sending in that question. Keep those requests coming, listeners tuning in to Audexa Radio. Stick around, we’ve got more news, conversation, and your questions coming up after this track.","type":"transition"}
]

[
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"We just got a call from a listener who wants to hear about tips for a first marathon, and I love this request! You’re tuning in to Audexa Radio, and wherever you are this morning—or whatever time of day you’re catching us—let’s get you ready to tackle those legendary 26.2 miles.","type":"listener_request"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Absolutely. The first big tip is to respect the distance. A marathon isn’t just a really long 5K; it’s an endurance project that rewards consistency, patience, and preparation. Ideally, give yourself several months to train, especially if you’re starting from a modest running base.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And please don’t make every training run a race. That’s a classic beginner mistake. Most of your runs should feel comfortable enough that you could hold a conversation—maybe not deliver a dramatic speech, Alex-style, but at least exchange a few sentences.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Exactly. A common approach is to run three or four times per week, gradually building weekly mileage. The long run is important, but increase distance carefully, and schedule easier weeks so your body can absorb the training. If pain changes your stride, keeps getting worse, or doesn’t improve with rest, don’t try to power through it—get medical advice.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Here’s another one: practice your race-day routine during training. Test your shoes, socks, clothing, breakfast, and hydration plan before the marathon. Race morning is not the moment to discover that your new shirt has the friction properties of sandpaper.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Fueling matters, too. During long runs, many athletes use carbohydrates from gels, chews, sports drinks, or other products they’ve already tested. Take fluids according to the conditions and your needs, but avoid suddenly overdrinking. Both dehydration and excessive water intake can be dangerous, so a training plan or qualified coach can help you find a sensible strategy.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"And don’t forget strength training. A couple of short sessions each week focusing on the legs, hips, core, and overall stability can support your running and help you handle the workload. Plus, recovery isn’t laziness—it’s part of the program. Sleep, easy days, and rest are where the adaptation happens.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"On race day, start slower than your excitement tells you to. The early miles often feel effortless because of the crowd and the adrenaline. Save energy for the second half, break the course into smaller sections, and remember that walking briefly at aid stations can be a smart pacing choice, not a failure.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"I love that: smart pacing, not surrender. And set more than one goal. Maybe your primary goal is finishing healthy, your second is sticking to a pacing plan, and your bonus goal is a time. That way, one tough patch doesn’t erase the whole achievement.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"Listen to your body, be flexible, and remember that completing a first marathon is already a major accomplishment. Training should challenge you, but it shouldn’t require ignoring serious symptoms or sacrificing your health.","type":"deep_dive"},
  {"speaker":"host1","text":"Great call, and thank you for giving us a chance to cheer on every first-time marathoner tuning in to Audexa Radio. Start gradually, train consistently, fuel wisely, and enjoy the journey—yes, even the long runs.","type":"outro"},
  {"speaker":"host2","text":"And remember, the finish line is only one part of the experience. Stick around, we’ve got more coming up after this track.","type":"transition"}
]

  {"speaker": "host1", "text": "Just poker-faced, no emotion whatsoever.", "type": "deep_dive"},
  {"speaker": "host2", "text": "None at all. Then Kuleshov intercut that identical facial shot with three different images: a bowl of hot soup, a little girl playing in a coffin, and a beautiful woman lounging on a sofa.", "type": "deep_dive"},

  {"speaker": "host1", "text": "Audexa Radio listeners, we just got a call from Marcus in Seattle who says he\u2019s been binging classic cinema docs and wants us to break down the history of the Kuleshov effect in film editing.   {"speaker": "host2", "text": "It\u2019s a perfect deep-dive subject. Lev Kuleshov was a Soviet filmmaker and teacher in the 1910s and 20s who basically proved that editing can create meaning that isn\u2019t literally on screen. His most famous experiment intercut the same neutral shot of actor Ivan Mozzhukhin\u2019s face with a bowl of soup, a dead child in a coffin, and a woman on a divan\u2014and audiences swore his expression changed every time.", "type": "deep_dive"},
  {"speaker": "host1", "text": "Wait, so the magic wasn\u2019t in the actor\u2019s performance at all\u2014it was the cut itself?", "type": "deep_dive"},
  {"speaker": "host2", "text": "Exactly. The footage of Mozzhukhin was identical each time; viewers projected the emotion onto him based on the juxtaposition. Kuleshov called it \u201ccreative geography\u201d\u2014the idea that two unrelated shots, when placed together, form a third idea in the viewer\u2019s mind.", "type": "deep_dive"},
  {"speaker": "host1", "text": "And this was happening right after the Russian Revolution, when film was still brand-new technology. How did that timing shape the theory?", "type": "deep_dive"},

His students included future legends like Eisenstein and Pudovkin, who pushed the technique even further.", "type": "deep_dive"},

  {"speaker": "host2", "text": "In a way, yes. Hitchcock\u2019s famous example of the bomb under the table is pure Kuleshov: suspense comes from what the audience knows is about to happen, not from anything the actors themselves are showing. The cut creates the dread.", "type": "deep_dive"},
  {"speaker": "host1", "text": "Mind-blowing. Marcus, we hope that scratched your cinema-history itch.
